name: Atlanta University
notes: The graduate center of the Atlanta group of colleges. Extensive collection of books and art on Negro culture in the Trevor Arnett Library, including the Hale Woodruff murals.

name: Benedict College
notes: A liberal arts college and school of theology. Points of interest: Antisdel Athletic Field, the new Dining Hall-Dormitory and Osborn Hall, oldest building on the campus.

name: Bennett College
notes: A woman's college of arts and sciences. Of interest: Annie Merner Pfeiffer Chapel, historic Bennett Bell, the Little Theatre, the Children's House.

name: Bethune-Cookman College
notes: A center of culture in the deep South. Sunday community programs open to visitors, 27 modern buildings on 169 acres. Founder Mary McLeod Bethune buried on campus.

name: Bishop College
notes: Point of interest: The C. H. Maxson Administration Building, a fine old mansion erected before the Civil War.

name: Clark College
notes: A co-educational member of the Atlanta University system. Point of interest: Merrill J. Holmes Hall, modern woman's dormitory.

name: Dillard University
notes: A 62-acre campus two miles northeast of New Orleans business district. Architecture a combination of Georgian and modified classic. Point of interest: the Flint-Goodridge Hospital.

name: Fisk University
notes: National reputation as a liberal arts college of high standing. Of special interest: the Alfred Stieglitz Collection of Art, the Carl Van Vechten Art Gallery, the Aaron Douglas Murals and the Balridge Collection of African Drawings in the Erastus Milo Cravath Memorial Library. Overnight visitors may reserve accommodations through Comptroller's Office.

name: Gammon Theological Seminary
notes: The Divinity School of the Atlanta University system. Points of interest: "Magnolia Drive," Gammon Hall, the Anna E. Hall dormitory.

name: Hampton Institute
notes: A 74-acre campus on the shores of historic Hampton Roads. Of special interest: the Collis P. Huntington Memorial Library with famed collection of books and pamphlets on Negro culture, the Henry O. Tanner paintings on religious themes, Ogden Hall, the modern Bemis Laboratories, Harkness Hall. Robert Russa Moton is buried here. Holly Tree Inn provides guest accommodations.

name: Huston-Tillotson College
notes: Formed by the merger of the two colleges of the Congregational and Methodist Churches. In process of developing a new modern campus.

name: Johnson C. Smith University
notes: 22 buildings on 75 acres. Points of interest: Biddle Hall, the James B. Duke Memorial Hall, the Henry Lawrence McCrorey Building, the Jane M. Smith Memorial Church.

name: Knoxville College
notes: Founded in 1863. Of special interest: the Young Memorial Fine Arts Building, the Giffen-Alumni Memorial Building.

name: Lane College
notes: Established in 1884 to serve youth of the C. M. E. Church. Named for its founder, Bishop Isaac Lane.

name: LeMoyne College
notes: Established before the close of the Civil War. Of interest: Brownlee Hall, Arthur Bruce Hall.

name: Lincoln University
notes: The oldest private Negro college. Established 1854. Of special interest: the Susan Reynolds Underhill Collection of African Art, Ashmun Hall (1856), Lincoln Hall (1866), the Vail Memorial Library. The Ladies Auxiliary Guest House provides overnight accommodations.

name: Livingstone College
notes: A campus of 316 acres. Of special interest: Hood Theological Seminary, Harris Hall. First president, Joseph Charles Price, buried here.

name: Morehouse College
notes: The men's college of the Atlanta University system. Of special interest: John Hope Monument, Graves Hall.

name: Morris Brown College
notes: A co-educational member of the Atlanta University system. Founded under patronage of the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

name: Paine College
notes: A winter-resort climate. Of special interest: Hoisey Hall, the Warren A. Candler Memorial Library.

name: Philander Smith College
notes: One of the oldest Negro colleges west of the Mississippi. Of interest: Old Budlong Hall, the modern science hall. Guest House accommodations available.

name: St. Augustine's College
notes: Small campus. Points of interest: St. Agnes Hospital Training School for Nurses, Bishop Tuttle School of Social Work, St. Augustine's Chapel, Benson Library, Atkinson Hall.

name: Shaw University
notes: Rich historic associations. Of special interest: Shaw Hall (1871), Estey Hall (1873), the Administration Building, the Art Gallery, Women's Recreation Building. Guest accommodations available in dormitories.

name: Spelman College
notes: The first college for Negro women in America. Point of interest: Sisters Chapel seating 1200 with three-manual pipe organ.

name: Talladega College
notes: Oldest college for Negroes in Alabama established 1867. Points of interest: the Hale Woodruff Murals in Savery Library, the Henry S. DeForest Chapel.

name: Texas College
notes: Located 100 miles east of Dallas. Of special interest: the Home Management House, Teacher's Aid Laboratory, Tea House with dining accommodations for visitors.

name: Tougaloo Southern Christian College
notes: A beautiful, rolling, wooded campus four miles north of Jackson. Points of interest: "The Mansion," built as planter's residence before Civil War. now home of president; Sarah A. Dickey Memorial Infirmary.

name: Tuskegee Institute
notes: Magnificent campus, 157 buildings on 4,925 acres. Of special interest: the George Washington Carver Museum, famed Booker T. Washington Monument, the Infantile Paralysis Pavilion of the John A. Andrews Hospital. Booker T. Washington and George Washington Carver buried on campus.

name: Virginia Union University
notes: The Belgian Friendship Building on the campus is a gift from the Belgian Government. Points of interest: the Robert L. Vann Tower, the William J. Clarke Library. Friday visitors may attend weekly campus convocations.

name: Wiley College
notes: Landscaped campus of 46 acres. Points of interest: The Sunken Garden, Brainard Chapel.

name: Xavier University
notes: A Catholic university, "New Xavier," was founded in 1915. Of special interest: three outstanding English Gothic structures of Indiana limestone, collection of French language books donated by the French government, and the Edward Morrell Memorial Collection of Bronzes.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Statue of Liberty
notes: Bartholdi's huge female figure of 'Liberty Enlightening the World,' presented to the United States by France in 1885. Figure, 151 ft. tall, tops 142 ft. pedestal. The copper statue alone weighs 225 tons. Circular stairway of 168 steps leads to interior of head. Boat to island leaves Pier A, Battery Place on the hour daily.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Fraunces Tavern
notes: Early Georgian colonial architecture. Museum of Revolutionary relics on second floor. Open 10-4 Mon. to Fri., 10-3 Sat. except during summer.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Wall Street
notes: The great financial center. At Nassau and Wall is Sub-Treasury Building on site of Federal Hall where George Washington took oath as first President of the United States. Admission free.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: United Nations World Capital
address: Along the East River, north of 42d St.
notes: Houses the Secretariat which is the 3,000-employee administrative organ of the United Nations, staffed by international civil servants. Meeting place of the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council and Trusteeship Council. For guided tour consult the Admissions Office.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: CHINA TOWN
notes: A short walk from City Hall and Brooklyn Bridge. Joss houses, curio shops and Chinese restaurants.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: ROOSEVELT HOUSE
notes: Birthplace and boyhood home of Theodore Roosevelt. Contains a collection of mementos of the President. Open weekdays, except Mon., 10-5; Sun. and holidays. Free.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: TIMES SQUARE
address: Intersection of Broadway, Seventh Ave. and 42nd St.
notes: Often called the “Great White Way” because of the brilliant “spectaculars,” flashing theatre marquees, shops, hotels and restaurants.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: EMPIRE STATE BUILDING
notes: Tallest structure in the world; 102 stories; 1,472 ft. high; 67 elevators. Observation terraces on 86th and 102d floors. Open 9:45 to midnight. Admission.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: ROCKEFELLER CENTER
address: 48th to 51st Streets between Fifth Avenue and Avenue of the Americas
notes: City-within-a-city. 15 skyscraper buildings occupy 12½ acres. Take a guided tour.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: CENTRAL PARK
address: 59th to 110th Sts., Fifth Avenue to Central Park West
notes: 2½ miles long, ½ mile wide. Contains the Mall, Zoo and Wollman Memorial; Central Park Lake with boats for hire; Cleopatra’s Needle. Horse drawn hacks may be hired for about $3.00 for the first half hour and $1 for every hour thereafter. Starting point 59th St. and Fifth Ave.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: HAYDEN PLANETARIUM
notes: “Theatre of the Stars” portrays the wonders of the sky. Performances daily. Admission charged.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: GRANT'S TOMB
notes: Massive granite memorial overlooking Hudson River containing the remains of General and Mrs. U. S. Grant.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Riverside Church
notes: Inter-denominational church resembles the 13th Century Cathedral of Chartres, France. The carillon, largest in the world, is housed at the top of a 22-story tower. The late Henry Burleigh was a featured vocalist there.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Coney Island
notes: Internationally known playground on Atlantic Ocean with 5 miles of bathing beach, boardwalk and amusements. Take BMT subway.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Bronx Zoo
address: Pelham Parkway & Bronx River Parkway Extension
notes: Largest in kinds and number of specimens in America. Contains a special zoo for children who are permitted to play with tame animals. Admission.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Hall of Fame
notes: The uptown campus of New York University is identified by the Hall of Fame. Contains eighty-three bronze busts and tablets of outstanding Americans. Booker T. Washington, the only Negro, was elected May, 1946. Sidney Barthe was the sculptor.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Jones Beach
notes: Reached via Meadowbrook and Wantagh State Parkways. From Harlem over the Triborough Bridge past La Guardia Airport. Features bathing in the Atlantic Ocean, Zachs Bay.

volume_title: Go, guide to pleasant motoring, Vol. 1
name: Franklin D. Roosevelt's Home
notes: Birthplace and burial site of the 32d President. Includes the Rose Garden and the Roosevelt Memorial Library (erected 1939).

name: Entry Fees and Equipment
notes: Tourist entering Canada are not required to pay entry fees, and may bring with them such articles of tourist outfits or sportsmen's equipment as they may require while in Canada for their own use and not for gain or hire, upon reporting same to the Customs Officer at the Canadaian frontier port of entry.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: Entering and Touring Mexico
notes: The only requirement is a simple permit issued at a cost of three pesos by the Mexican customs upon crossing the border at Nuevo Laredo. This permit may also be obtained in Laredo, Texas, at the branch office of the A. A. A. at the corner of Matamoros St. and Convent Ave. Your car registration certificate is necessary for purpose of identification. No special driving license is required other than on issued to you by your particular state; this you should keep in your car or on your person at all times when driving in Mexico.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: NOTE
notes: Do not discard any car equipment while in Mexico—such as old tires, broken bumpers, etc.,—or you will probably be required to pay duty on such missing items upon leaving Mexico.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: DRIVING PRECAUTIONS
notes: All road signs are in Spanish. If you cannot get a folder and do not understand the meaning of a road sign, check your speed there is something ahead which requires attention, because most highways in Mexico are not fenced and livestock is often found on the road; therefore excessive driving speeds around curves or places where the view is obstructed is very dangerous. In the mountain region, especially between Tamazunchale and Zimapan, heavy fogs are occasionally encountered. When the atmosphere becomes so dense that vision ahead is obscured it is wise to pull off to the side of the road as far as possible and wait with your lights on for a few minutes for the fog to lift.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: HOTELS
notes: First class hotels may be found everywhere in Mexico along the travel routes. Prices are reasonable. Excellent food in both American and European style can be obtained practically everywhere.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: MEXICAN CUSTOMS REGULATIONS
notes: Visitors entering Mexico as tourist may bring in any reasonable amount of clothing, sporting goods camping outfits, cameras, forty packages of cigarette, 100 cigars or a pound of tobacco free of duty. Upon arrival at the Custom Office, all baggage must be removed from the car for inspection. (Registered porters will do this work for you for a small tip.) Most of the attendants speak english so you will have no difficulty. If you have your Tourist Card and auto permit, there are no cost of any kind. These formalities are completed in a few minutes.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: U. S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS
notes: You are permitted to bring back merchandise up to a value of $100.00, free of duty, when intended for personal use or gifts, others may be imported only upon payments of duty, because of patent and trade-mark restrictions, however the exceptions are rare, yet a few brands of perfume are included in this category, if you intend to purchase perfume it is best to buy at reliable stores familiar with the U. S. customs requirement. Importation of liquors under the $100.00 exemption are limited to a one gallon. Residents of dry states cannot bring in liquor. Texas residents one quart. Certain other states have regulatory laws and taxes affecting all liquors brought into such states. If you intend to bring back liquor with you, it is best to check the liquor regulations of your own state before leaving.

volume_title: Smith's tourist guide of necessary information for businessman, tourist, traveler and vacationist
name: SPECIAL NOTE
notes: Should you carry with you into Mexico any articles of foreign make, such as cameras, binoculars, or any articles of unusual value, or whose origin cannot easily be proved they should be recorded at the U. S. Customs Office in Laredo, before you enter Mexico. A certificate listing such articles will be given you, without charge, which will protect you against argument or payment of duty upon your return to the United States.
